simple: the small file that knows the addresses of one board's devices.
analogy: the building plan pinned in the caretaker's office: which switch is which.
precise: the code that maps a specific board's peripherals (base addresses, register layouts, pin choices) to functions the application calls; vendor kits ship large ones, this course writes a minimal one (board.h).
source: D3 of F3-36 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a list of functions that set up global C++ objects before main.
analogy: the list of rooms whose lights must be switched on before school opens.
precise: an array of function pointers that the compiler emits in a section named .init_array, one per translation unit with dynamically initialised globals; a hosted C++ run-time calls them before main, and on bare metal your start-up code must.
source: D4, D5 of F3-36 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open); R1 of F3-36 (lab runs in this build)

simple: the program that lives permanently inside a device and runs it.
analogy: the caretaker who opens the building every morning and, in a small school, also runs the whole day.
precise: software stored in a device's non-volatile memory (flash on a microcontroller) and executed directly by its processor from reset, here without any operating system underneath it.
source: D3 of F3-36 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how much flash and RAM your program may use, and how much it does use.
analogy: the number of cupboards and desks the school has, against how many the timetable needs.
precise: flash use = code + read-only data + constructor table + the stored initial values of .data; RAM use = .data + .bss + the stack (and heap, if any); both must be at most the chip's sizes from its datasheet.
source: D4 of F3-36 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open); R1 of F3-36 (lab runs in this build)

simple: a way for firmware to ask the debugger or emulator for a service, such as "stop now and report success".
analogy: the caretaker phoning the head office from the school's single telephone.
precise: an Arm convention in which the target executes a special breakpoint (bkpt 0xab on Armv7-M) with an operation number in r0 and an argument in r1, and the host side (debugger or emulator) performs the operation; here it is used only for SYS_EXIT.
source: D6 of F3-36 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open); R1 of F3-36 (lab runs in this build)

simple: the first code that runs, which prepares memory so that normal C++ works.
analogy: the caretaker's morning round before the first lesson.
precise: the reset handler and its helpers: copy initial values of .data from flash to RAM, zero .bss, run the constructors listed in .init_array, then call main.
source: D2, D5 of F3-36 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the lowest bit of a code address on Cortex-M, which must be 1.
analogy: a tick on the room card that says "speak the school's language here".
precise: Armv7-M executes only the Thumb instruction set; addresses loaded into the program counter from the vector table or by a branch-and-exchange carry bit 0 = 1 to mark Thumb state, so a function at 0x84 appears as 0x85 in the vector table.
source: D1 of F3-36 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open); R1 of F3-36 (lab runs in this build)

simple: telling the device "I have seen your interrupt" so it stops asking.
analogy: switching off the doorbell's lamp after opening the door.
precise: a write to the peripheral's interrupt-clear register (often write-1-to-clear) that de-asserts its interrupt request; on a level-sensitive line, a handler that returns without it is entered again at once.
source: D2 of F3-37 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open); R3 of F3-37 (lab runs in this build)

simple: making a bus protocol by switching pins in software.
analogy: tapping Morse code by hand instead of using a telegraph machine.
precise: driving and sampling the lines of a serial protocol directly from software through GPIO-like registers, so timing is set by the code; the alternative is a dedicated controller peripheral that generates the waveform.
source: D3 of F3-37 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: two ways of counting the same interrupt.
analogy: room 24 on the school plan is "the eighth classroom".
precise: on Armv7-M, exception numbers 1–15 are the core's own (reset, faults, SVCall, PendSV, SysTick) and external interrupt n has exception number 16 + n, which is also its vector-table word index; the active exception number is readable in the IPSR register.
source: D1 of F3-37 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open); R1 of F3-37 (lab runs in this build)

simple: one conversation on the two-wire bus, from "start" to "stop".
analogy: knocking, saying the room number and "I want to tell you" or "I want to ask you", then talking, with a nod after every sentence.
precise: a START condition (SDA falls while SCL is high), a byte of 7-bit address plus R/W bit, an ACK bit from the addressed target, data bytes each followed by ACK or NACK, optionally a repeated START to change direction, and a STOP (SDA rises while SCL is high).
source: D5 of F3-37 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open); R2 of F3-37 (lab runs in this build)

simple: an interrupt that fires again and again so fast that nothing else runs.
analogy: a doorbell stuck down: the caretaker never gets back to her desk.
precise: a condition in which an interrupt source stays asserted (for example, never acknowledged) so the core re-enters its handler continuously and lower-priority code, including main, is starved.
source: R3 of F3-37 (lab runs in this build)

simple: an event that happened but whose interrupt never ran its handler.
analogy: the caretaker switches off the lamp after closing the door, at the very moment a second visitor rings: that ring is erased.
precise: a race in which a new event's pending flag is cleared by software that meant to clear an older one, or arrives while the source is masked and is not latched; the data waits, but no interrupt announces it.
source: R4 of F3-37 (lab runs in this build)

simple: the interrupt controller built into every Cortex-M core.
analogy: the office panel of lamps, one per doorbell, with a rule for which lamp wins.
precise: the Armv7-M interrupt controller, memory-mapped from 0xE000E100, with per-line enable (ISER/ICER), pending (ISPR/ICPR), active and priority registers; it presents the highest-priority pending enabled interrupt to the core, which fetches the handler address from the vector table ("vectored") and may pre-empt a lower-priority handler ("nested").
source: D1, D2 of F3-37 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: starting a new conversation without letting go of the bus.
analogy: "and now a question" without leaving the room.
precise: a START condition sent instead of a STOP, so that the controller keeps the bus while switching from writing a register pointer to reading that register.
source: D5 of F3-37 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a circular queue between one writer and one reader.
analogy: a pigeon-hole rack by the door: the caretaker puts letters in, the teacher takes them out, each moving only their own marker.
precise: a fixed array with a head index written only by the producer (here the interrupt handler) and a tail index written only by the consumer (here main); with single-word index stores and correct ordering of data and index, it needs no lock on a single core.
source: D3, D4 of F3-37 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the fixed 8-byte message a simple keyboard sends.
analogy: a pre-printed form even a substitute teacher can read.
precise: a report of one modifier byte (Ctrl, Shift, Alt, GUI bits), one reserved byte and six key-usage bytes, defined so that BIOS/UEFI firmware can use a keyboard without parsing report descriptors.
source: D2 of F3-38 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open); R1 of F3-38 (lab runs in this build)

simple: the full CV, with a number on the first line saying how long it is.
analogy: "this CV has 34 pages": if the number is wrong, the secretary stops reading early.
precise: a 9-byte header followed by all interface, class-specific and endpoint descriptors of that configuration; its wTotalLength field is the length of the whole set, which the host uses to read it in a second request.
source: D1 of F3-38 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open); R2 of F3-38 (lab runs in this build)

simple: a question-and-answer exchange on endpoint 0.
analogy: the secretary's form: question, the visitor's written answer, a stamp that closes the exchange.
precise: a transfer of three stages: a SETUP stage carrying an 8-byte request (bmRequestType, bRequest, wValue, wIndex, wLength), an optional data stage in the direction given by bmRequestType, and a status stage in the opposite direction with a zero-length packet.
source: D1 of F3-38 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open); R1 of F3-38 (lab runs in this build)

simple: a one-bit sequence number on each data packet.
analogy: alternating red and blue envelopes: a repeated colour means "you already have this one".
precise: data packets alternate between the DATA0 and DATA1 packet IDs per endpoint, so that a receiver can detect a retransmission after a lost handshake; a SETUP stage always uses DATA0, and the data stage of a control transfer starts with DATA1.
source: D1 of F3-38 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the 18-byte identity card of a USB device.
analogy: the visitor's short card.
precise: the first descriptor a host reads: USB version, device class, maximum packet size of endpoint 0, vendor and product IDs, device release, string indices and the number of configurations.
source: D1, D3 of F3-38 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a numbered mailbox inside the device, with a direction.
analogy: the pigeon-hole the secretary checks every ten minutes.
precise: a uniquely addressable source or sink of data in a device, identified by number and direction (bit 7 of bEndpointAddress: 1 = IN, device to host); each has a transfer type (control, interrupt, bulk, isochronous) and a maximum packet size.
source: D1 of F3-38 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the standard way keyboards, mice and similar devices talk, so the PC needs no special driver.
analogy: "a keyboard teacher: we have a standard room for those".
precise: a USB device class (interface class 3) whose devices describe their data format in a report descriptor and send reports over an interrupt IN endpoint; operating systems ship a generic driver for it.
source: D2 of F3-38 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a small program-like table that tells the PC what each byte of a report means.
analogy: the legend of a map.
precise: a sequence of HID items (usage page, usage, logical minimum and maximum, report size and count, input/output/feature, collections) that defines the layout and meaning of the device's reports.
source: D2 of F3-38 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the firmware that makes a microcontroller behave as a USB device.
analogy: the visitor's folder of prepared answers and the habit of answering only when asked.
precise: device-side software layered over the chip's USB device controller: endpoint 0 request handling (standard, class and vendor requests), descriptor storage, and class drivers (HID, CDC, mass storage) that feed data endpoints; TinyUSB is an open example.
source: D1, D4 of F3-38 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: putting one task aside and continuing another exactly where it stopped.
analogy: one group leaves the hall with a note of where they were in their practice; the next group picks up from its own note.
precise: saving the running task's registers (here partly by the exception hardware, partly by the kernel) on its stack, storing its stack pointer in its TCB, selecting the next task, and restoring that task's stack pointer and registers.
source: D1 of F3-39 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open); R1 of F3-39 (lab runs in this build)

simple: the most urgent ready task always runs, and takes over at once when it becomes ready.
analogy: the rule on the hall door.
precise: a scheduling policy in which each task has a static priority, the scheduler always dispatches the highest-priority ready task, and a task becoming ready with a higher priority than the running one causes an immediate switch.
source: D4 of F3-39 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an Armv7-M exception that software raises to say "switch tasks when nothing more urgent is running".
analogy: a note on the hall door: "change groups at the next break".
precise: the pendable service call, exception 14, made pending by setting ICSR bit 28; given the lowest priority, it runs only after every other handler has finished, which makes it the standard place for the context switch on Cortex-M.
source: D1, D2 of F3-39 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the task that must run most often gets the highest priority.
analogy: the group that comes back most often goes first.
precise: for periodic tasks with deadlines equal to periods, assigning priorities in order of period (shorter period, higher priority); it is optimal among fixed-priority assignments for that task model.
source: D4, D5 of F3-39 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a formula that predicts each task's worst response time before you run anything.
analogy: working out on paper the latest any group could finish.
precise: for fixed-priority preemptive scheduling of independent periodic tasks, the worst-case response time Ri is the smallest solution of Ri = Ci + Σj more urgent ⌈Ri / Tj⌉ · Cj, found by iteration starting at Ri = Ci; C is the worst-case execution time, T the period.
source: D4 of F3-39 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open); R2 of F3-39 (lab runs in this build)

simple: how long a job takes from "it is due" to "it is done", and the latest it may be done.
analogy: from the bell that calls the group to the moment they finish; their deadline is the next bell.
precise: a job's response time is its completion time minus its release time; a job meets its deadline if its response time is at most its relative deadline (here equal to the period). The worst-case response time is the maximum over all jobs.
source: D4 of F3-39 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a small operating system whose main promise is "on time", not "fast on average".
analogy: the hall rule plus the person who enforces it.
precise: a kernel that provides tasks, a priority-based preemptive scheduler, timing services and synchronisation objects, designed so that the worst-case delay of each operation is bounded and can be analysed; on microcontrollers it is linked into one image with the application, usually without memory protection between tasks.
source: D2, D3 of F3-39 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the kernel's record card for one task.
analogy: the group's line on the hall booking sheet.
precise: the kernel data structure holding a task's saved stack pointer, priority, state and timing fields; in this course's kernel it is os::Task, whose first member is the saved stack pointer so that assembly code can reach it at offset 0.
source: R1 of F3-39 (lab runs in this build)

simple: one independent job of the firmware, with its own loop.
analogy: one group that needs the hall.
precise: a thread of execution with its own stack and saved registers, a priority and a state (ready, running, blocked or sleeping); RTOSes call it a task (FreeRTOS) or a thread (Zephyr).
source: D3, D6 of F3-39 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the fraction of processor time the tasks need.
analogy: how much of the week the hall is booked.
precise: U = Σ Ci / Ti; U ≤ 1 is necessary for any schedule to work, and U ≤ n(21/n − 1) is a sufficient (not necessary) test for rate-monotonic scheduling of n tasks (the Liu and Layland bound).
source: D4, D5 of F3-39 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a task that waits for something other than time.
analogy: the exam group standing at the locked door.
precise: the scheduling state of a task waiting on a kernel object (a mutex to be released, a message to arrive); it is not eligible to run until the object's operation wakes it. In uRTOS v2: State::Blocked with waitingOn naming the object.
source: R1 of F3-40 (lab runs in this build)

simple: a text file that describes the board's hardware, from which Zephyr generates configuration for its drivers.
analogy: the school's building plan that every new staff member receives.
precise: a hierarchical description of hardware (nodes, compatible strings, registers, interrupts, pin assignments) in devicetree source; Zephyr compiles it at build time into C macros that drivers and applications use, the same format the Linux kernel reads at boot on many Arm systems (Track D).
source: D3 of F3-40 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the list of on/off and number settings that choose which RTOS features are built.
analogy: the school's policy checklist: "do we run a canteen? how many classrooms?".
precise: the configuration language (from the Linux kernel) that Zephyr uses for build-time options such as enabling a subsystem or setting the tick rate; FreeRTOS uses a header, FreeRTOSConfig.h, for the same purpose.
source: D3, D4 of F3-40 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: something the RTOS gives tasks to cooperate with: a mutex, a queue, a semaphore, an event flag, a timer.
analogy: the school's shared things with rules attached: the lab key, the pigeon-holes, the bell.
precise: a kernel-managed data structure with operations that may block the calling task and wake others, implemented with interrupts disabled (or a kernel lock) so its state changes are atomic with respect to the scheduler.
source: D3, D4 of F3-40 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a kernel-owned mailbox of fixed-size messages between tasks.
analogy: pigeon-holes with a rule: a reader with nothing to read waits by them.
precise: a bounded FIFO of fixed-size items whose send and receive operations can block (receive when empty, send when full, depending on options) and wake the waiting task; the usual way to pass data from a producer task (or interrupt) to a consumer task without sharing variables.
source: D3, D4 of F3-40 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: while you hold what an urgent task needs, you become as urgent as it.
analogy: lending the young class the exam group's badge until they return the key.
precise: a mutex protocol in which the owner's effective priority is raised to the highest priority of the tasks blocked on the mutex, and restored when it unlocks; it bounds the blocking time to the length of the owner's critical section (per resource, for non-nested use).
source: D1 of F3-40 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open); R1 of F3-40 (lab runs in this build)

simple: an urgent task waits for a less urgent one, and a middle task delays them both.
analogy: the exam group waits for the young class, which is stuck in the middle years' assembly.
precise: a situation in which a high-priority task is blocked on a resource held by a low-priority task, which in turn is preempted by medium-priority tasks that do not need the resource; the high-priority task's blocking time then depends on the medium tasks' execution and is unbounded in general.
source: D1 of F3-40 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open); R2 of F3-40 (lab runs in this build)

simple: write the new firmware next to the old one, then switch.
analogy: prepare the second classroom while the first is in use.
precise: an update scheme with two image slots in which the running image is never modified; the new image is written to the other slot, and a small, atomic state change makes the boot loader select it.
source: D1 of F3-41 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open); R1 of F3-41 (lab runs in this build)

simple: refusing to install an older version, even a correctly signed one.
analogy: last year's timetable, still signed, must not come back.
precise: a check that an image's version (or security counter) is at least a stored minimum, which is raised when a newer image is confirmed; it stops an attacker from installing an old, signed image with a known vulnerability.
source: D1 of F3-41 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open); R1 of F3-41 (lab runs in this build)

simple: a small program that runs first, checks the real firmware and starts it.
analogy: the person who unlocks the classroom and lets the principal in, after checking the appointment letter.
precise: firmware placed at the reset vector that selects, validates and starts an application image stored elsewhere in flash, and on many designs also installs updates; it is rarely updated itself, so its correctness matters more than any application's.
source: D1, D3 of F3-41 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a device that no longer starts and cannot fix itself.
analogy: the school standing in the corridor with no timetable.
precise: a device whose boot path finds no runnable image and offers no recovery that works in the field, so it needs physical intervention (a debug probe, a factory programmer) or replacement.
source: R2 of F3-41 (lab runs in this build)

simple: a 32-byte fingerprint of data; change one bit and the fingerprint changes completely.
analogy: a seal across every page of the timetable.
precise: a function from any byte string to a fixed-size digest, designed so that finding two inputs with the same digest, or an input for a given digest, is infeasible; SHA-256 (FIPS 180-4) gives 256 bits. It detects accidental and deliberate changes, but anyone can compute it, so it does not prove who made the image.
source: D5 of F3-41 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open); R3 of F3-41 (lab runs in this build)

simple: proof that the image was approved by whoever holds a secret key.
analogy: the principal's signature, which the door-keeper checks against a sample kept in the office.
precise: a value computed from the image with a private key that anyone holding the matching public key can verify, and nobody without the private key can produce; Ed25519 is one signature scheme (RFC 8032). The boot loader stores only the public key.
source: D6 of F3-41 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open); R1 of F3-41 (lab runs in this build)

simple: a fixed area of flash that can hold one complete firmware image.
analogy: one classroom.
precise: a flash partition sized for an image (header, code and data, metadata such as signatures), addressed by the boot loader; designs have one slot (overwrite in place) or two (primary/secondary, A/B).
source: D1 of F3-41 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an open-source secure boot loader for microcontrollers.
analogy: a professional door-keeper service that many schools hire.
precise: a boot loader project that validates signed images in primary and secondary slots and supports several upgrade strategies (including swapping slots with test-and-confirm, and overwrite), used with Zephyr and other RTOSes; its image format and tools are outside this build's verification.
source: D1 of F3-41 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the new firmware gets one try; it must say "I'm fine" or the old one comes back.
analogy: the trial day in the new classroom.
precise: the boot loader starts a newly installed image once, marked as on trial; the image must mark itself confirmed (after self-tests) before the next reset, otherwise the boot loader reverts to the previous image.
source: D1 of F3-41 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open); R1 of F3-41 (lab runs in this build)

simple: the register that tells the core where the vector table is.
analogy: moving the card on the door to the new classroom.
precise: an Armv7-M system control register at 0xE000ED08 holding the base address of the active vector table; a boot loader writes the application's table address there before jumping, so that the application's interrupts reach its own handlers.
source: D2 of F3-41 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open); R3 of F3-41 (lab runs in this build)

simple: the agreed way for the operating system to ask the EC for a byte or give it one.
analogy: the hatch with an in-tray and an out-tray.
precise: a pair of one-byte I/O registers, a status/command register and a data register, with commands such as read, write and query, and status bits for "input buffer full", "output buffer full" and "event pending"; the platform's ACPI tables tell the OS where the registers are and what the EC's bytes mean.
source: D1 of F3-42 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: small programs, supplied by the laptop maker, that the operating system runs to learn what the EC's bytes mean.
analogy: the instruction sheet pinned beside the hatch.
precise: bytecode in the platform's ACPI tables, interpreted by the OS; for the EC it defines fields in the EC's address space and methods such as battery status and event handlers, so the same OS driver works on laptops with different EC layouts.
source: D1 of F3-42 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a separate small computer on a server's main board that can switch the server on and off and watch its health, even when the server is off.
analogy: the night watchman with his own keys and phone line.
precise: a system-on-chip with its own processor, memory, firmware and network port, powered from standby power, that controls host power, reads sensors, drives fans, logs events and offers a remote console; reachable from the host (in band) and over the network (out of band).
source: D4, C1 of F3-42 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a small computer inside a laptop that looks after the keyboard, battery, fans and lid.
analogy: the school caretaker.
precise: a microcontroller on the motherboard with its own firmware, running whenever the board has power (including in sleep states), which scans the keyboard matrix, talks to the battery and charger over SMBus, controls fans and power sequencing, and exposes data and events to the operating system through the ACPI Embedded Controller interface.
source: D1, C1 of F3-42 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: two flags: "the EC has not yet taken your byte" and "the EC has put a byte for you".
analogy: a note still in the in-tray; a paper waiting in the out-tray.
precise: status bits that synchronise the two sides: the host must wait for IBF clear before writing and for OBF set before reading; reading the data register clears OBF.
source: D1 of F3-42 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open); R1 of F3-42 (lab runs in this build)

simple: an older standard set of messages for talking to a BMC.
analogy: the watchman's fixed list of radio codes.
precise: the Intelligent Platform Management Interface: request messages with a network function (netfn) and command number plus data, answered by a response with netfn + 1, the same command, a completion code and data; carried in band (for example the KCS interface) or out of band over the LAN.
source: D4, D5 of F3-42 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: managing a machine through a path that does not need the machine's own operating system.
analogy: phoning the watchman instead of the school office.
precise: access to a management controller over its own network port or a dedicated channel, independent of host power and host software; it works on a crashed or powered-off host, and it is also an attack surface that bypasses the host's defences.
source: D4 of F3-42 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the newer way to manage servers, over the same web technology browsers use.
analogy: the watchman now also answers e-mail with a fixed form.
precise: a DMTF standard for management over HTTPS with JSON resources, which many BMCs offer beside or instead of IPMI.
source: D6 of F3-42 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the EC's way of saying "something happened, ask me what".
analogy: the caretaker rings the office bell; the clerk comes to the hatch and asks.
precise: the EC sets an event bit and raises a system control interrupt; the OS sends the query command, receives an event number and runs the ACPI method that the platform's tables associate with that number.
source: D1 of F3-42 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a slow two-wire bus that the EC uses to talk to the battery.
analogy: the caretaker's walkie-talkie to the boiler room.
precise: the System Management Bus, a two-wire bus derived from I2C with defined transactions and timeouts; smart batteries report remaining capacity, full capacity, voltage and more over it.
source: D3 of F3-42 (pending verification; sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)
